name: Graph Plotting
description: Learn about Graph Plotting and its applications in physics.

content.overview: Here's a fun fact: your brain is way better at spotting a trend in a picture than in a wall of numbers. That's basically the whole reason graphs exist. A table full of numbers hides its patterns; the same numbers on a graph practically shout them at you. {{viz:diagram-01}}
content.explanation:
Let's turn that spring-height table from before into something your eyes can actually process. A good graph needs a few key ingredients:

**1. A title.** What is this graph even showing? 'Temperature vs Spring Height' tells you right away.

**2. Axis labels with units.** 'Temperature (°C)' on one axis, 'Height (mm)' on the other. Never leave people guessing.

**3. A sensible scale.** Use the full space on both axes—don't cram all your points into one tiny corner like you're hiding them.

**4. Plot your points carefully.** Mark each one precisely—dots, X's, whatever, just be accurate.

**5. Connect with lines when it makes sense.** Tested 20°C, 25°C, 30°C? Draw a line through them to show the trend—don't just leave scattered dots floating there. {{viz:formula-01}}

**Here's why this actually matters:**
- Table: 20→15, 25→18, 30→21.5 (fine, but you have to squint)
- Graph: instantly you see 'as temperature goes up, height climbs steadily'—way clearer, right? {{viz:chart-01}}

**A few graph types worth knowing:**
- **Scatter plot:** just dots, no lines. Use it when your data's noisy or you're not sure there's a real relationship yet.
- **Line graph:** dots connected with lines. Use it once you're confident about the trend.
- **Bar graph:** great for comparing categories, like Spring A vs B vs C.

A good graph basically tells the story of your data before you even say a word.
keyPoints: Give it a clear title and labeled axes (with units!)
Use a sensible scale—fill the space, don't crowd it into a corner
Connect with lines when the trend actually makes sense
A graph reveals patterns that raw numbers hide
Pick the right graph type for the data you've got
content.whyItMatters: Graphs let you—and anyone else looking at your work—see what your data actually means in about two seconds flat, instead of squinting at a spreadsheet.
